prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: the lamp or bright foreground object at the lower edge is nearest (about 0.2–0.6 m), the drum kit is roughly 0.7–1.8 m ahead, and the sofa, chairs, walls, and other room surfaces are farther away (about 2–5 m). It separates overlapping drum components more clearly than RGB: cymbals sit above the drums, the nearer drums and stands occlude parts of the kit, and the furniture remains behind it; the person/arm entering near the middle frames is also closer than most of the kit and within the camera wearer's arm's reach. Across the five frames the principal depth layers stay stable while the viewpoint shifts laterally and turns slightly, causing the kit and foreground lamp to slide across the image rather than clearly approach or retreat. Exact metric distances, thin stands, reflective cymbals, the glowing lamp, frame boundaries, and the partially visible person are unreliable because monocular depth is smooth, relative, and affected by glare and occlusion.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates only a few foreground instances: a person-shaped region appears near the right edge of frame 1, near the center-right of frame 3, partly along the top of frame 4, and at the far right of frame 5, while frame 2 has no clear detection. These masks show that the person is only partly in view and shifts around the camera wearer across time, but they do not establish the person's full body position, facing direction, gaze, or distance; where visible, the person appears close, approximately 0.3–1.2 m away and likely within arm's reach. The map makes the changing occlusion and truncation of that nearby person easier to see than RGB, but it omits the drum kit, cymbals, furniture, and most other objects, so distances and relations among those objects must come from RGB or depth. The small region labelled "banana" at the extreme left of frame 1 is inconsistent with the RGB scene and is likely a false detection, and the fragmented person masks are too incomplete to infer whether the person approaches, retreats, turns, or looks toward the camera wearer.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only a magenta hand skeleton in frame 3, positioned slightly right of center and above the lower edge, with no reliable body skeleton or pose detections in the other four frames. In RGB context, that hand is in front of the drum kit and appears close to the camera wearer, roughly 0.3–0.8 m away and within arm's reach, while the drums remain farther ahead at roughly 0.7–1.8 m. The skeleton reveals finger and hand orientation more clearly than the dark, cluttered RGB frame, with the hand extending upward and slightly right, but it provides no dependable evidence about a person's full-body facing direction, gaze, position behind the camera, or distance to another person. Because the hand is detected in only one frame and no body is recovered, temporal approach, retreat, or turning cannot be established, and the tightly clustered joints may be distorted by occlusion, motion blur, or low light.
